newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Experts debate repairs to holed Mir space module.
newsitem.headline: Experts debate repairs to holed Mir space module.

text.p: Russian and American experts held urgent talks at mission control near Moscow on Thursday to map out how the crew of the Mir space station can repair damage from the worst accident in its 11-year history.

One of the three-man Russian-American crew may have to make an emergency space walk to try to plug a hole punctured in one of Mir's modules on Wednesday and repair a solar panel whose loss has cut the station's power supply.

A meeting of a 72-strong expert committee, which includes Mir's chief designer and representatives of the U.S. space agency NASA, began at 0930 GMT at the Korolyov mission control centre outside the Russian capital.
Throughout the Moscow morning the crew held intensive discussions with specialists on the ground during 20- to 30-minute periods of radio contact.
"It's possible to go through into the (damaged) module in a spacesuit," one of the two Russians told mission control. Officials had said earlier a space walk might be necessary.

Film showed a smooth round hole several centimetres wide in the wall of the Spektr module, which was sealed off along with considerable quantities of equipment. It lost its air after being pierced by the docking probe from an unmanned Progress cargo craft during manual training manoevres.

The cosmonaut -- poor sound quality meant reporters could not tell if it was Vasily Tsibliyev or Alexander Lazutkin -- also added that he thought the broken solar panel could be reached. The film showed about a fifth of its surface missing.

The collision, apart from stranding U.S. astronaut Michael Foale's personal belongings in the stricken module, also knocked the station out of alignment, forcing the crew to reposition it to catch the Sun's rays and restore some electricity.

Reporters, who saw no pictures of the crew, heard the cosmonauts laugh. British-born Foale could be heard saying, "OK, OK," in reply to a stream of inaudible questions from a NASA representative at mission control.
In an earlier exchange, reporters at Mission Control heard Tsibliyev asking: "Should we switch on button B2?"
"Yes, try it," replied Mission Control. "What's the result?"
"Then try it again," came the voice of the expert.
Officials insist the cosmonauts are in no danger and note that a Soyuz-T spacecraft is docked on Mir to be used as a lifeboat in emergencies. It could return them to Earth.

But the launch of a relief craft, originally a routine supply mission planned for Friday, was set to be postponed, awaiting the arrival of a small section of specialised power cable needed to patch up Mir's damaged electricity system.

The cable could take two to three days to reach the launch site at Baikonur. The unmanned Progress cargo craft, similar to the one involved in the collision, may also be loaded with other supplies needed for the repairs.
Even when it arrives, however, a spokesman for Russia's Military Space Forces told Reuters that the loss of power on Mir would make the docking of the new Progress "very difficult".
The incident, which follows a fire on Mir in February and a number of other mishaps, has raised fresh doubts about the safety of Russia's financially troubled space programme.
A senior U.S. Congressman has urged NASA to review safety before any more U.S. astronauts go on board for a long stay.
